caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 304 of 2004 with Civil Rule No. 645(FM) of 2004
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam with AQM Shafiullah, Advocates ----- For the Appellants. 
Rafique-ul-Huq with Ahsanul Karim, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
IFIC Bank Ltd and others ------ Appellants
vs
Beximco Holdings Ltd and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendants presented the appeal against an order dated 27-10-2004 passed by Joint District Judge, Court No.5 in Dhaka in Title Suit No. 191 of 2004, which granted temporary injunction restraining the defendants from sending names of the plaintiffs to the Bangladesh Bank for publication in the CIB (Credit Information Bureau) report. 

 2. Short facts for disposal of the appeal are that on 31-8-04 respondent No. 1 Messrs Beximco Holding Company Ltd, in short, Beximco Holdings, and four others as plaintiffs instituted thy suit against the International Finance Investment and Commerce Bank Ltd, in short, the IFIC Bank, and others for a decree of several declarations including the ones that no amount was due from the plaintiffs to the defendants under the schedule 112 accounts and the Baghkhali Fisheries Ltd under section 47 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, briefly, the Ain, and that no suit could be filed by the defendants against the plaintiffs since any claim became barred under section 46 of the Ain and also for a perpetual injunction for restraining the defendants from showing the plaintiffs defaulter in anyway or anywhere. 

 3. Plaint case, in short, is that under the schedule accounts said IFIC Bank advanced about Taka 55,00,00,000 and they already paid up more than 300 percent of said principal amount. Any further claim under those accounts would be barred under sections 46 and/or 47 of the Ain. But said IFIC Bank sent a legal notice on 18-4-04 to the plaintiffs demanding Taka 135,09,69,533.31 claiming due as on 31-12-03 

 4. In the circumstances, the plaintiffs on 2-9-04 made an application under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from showing the plaintiffs as defaulter and/or supplying their names to the Bangladesh Bank for publication in the CIB report. 

 5. Pursuant to the summons, the defendants appeared and opposed the application by filing a written objection. They contended that plaintiff Beximco Holdings obtained advances/loans against schedule 112 accounts in the names of fictitious persons from different branches of the IFIC Bank. On detection of those loan accounts, the Beximco Holdings by board resolution dated 12-12-93 admitted and acknowledged their liabilities of outstanding dues as against those 112 loan accounts and resolved that the Beximco Holdings shall undertake to pay Taka 118,46,37,087.31 as on 30-9- 93 with interest and other charges. They authorised the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 Chairman and Managing Director and Vice-Chairman and Director of the Beximco Holdings to sign and execute the guarantee for repayment of said outstanding dues for and on behalf of the Beximco Holdings. Accordingly, plaintiff Nos. 2 to 5 being directors of the Beximco Holdings took responsibilities to execute personnel guarantees in addition to corporate guarantee for said outstanding dues. As per said Board resolution, the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 furnished the letter of guarantee on the same date as security for repayment of the loan liabilities on behalf of the Beximco Holdings. After such re-schedulement, the Beximco Holdings paid Taka 13,00,00.000 being installments from 1-1-98 to 31-1-99 at the rate of Taka 1,00,00,000 per month. They paid Taka 1,00,00,000 per month from 28-2- 99 to 31-12-2000. They also paid Taka 2,00,00,000 from 31-1-01 to 31-1-02. Thereafter, the Beximco Holdings failed to pay any installment but deposited Taka 40,00,000 only on 29-4-2002 as down payment along with an application for further re-schedulement of the outstanding liabilities. 

 6. After several correspondences, defendant No. 2 served a legal notice upon the plaintiffs calling upon them to liquidate the outstanding dues of Taka 135,09,69,535.31 with interest as was due on 30-12-03 within one month from date of receipt of the notice. The plaintiffs though received the legal notice on 26-2-04 but did not take any step for repayment. Then, the IFIC Bank served a statutory notice under section 9(2) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 upon the plaintiffs on 18-1-04 which they duly received on 20-4-04. After the expiry of statutory period of 90 days, the plaintiffs did not bother to pay. Then, the IFIC was constrained to institute a suit being Bankruptcy Suit No. 88 of 2004 on 26-7-04 in the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka. 

 7. It also denied that the plaintiffs already paid 300% of the principal amount. 

 8. By impugned order, learned Joint District Judge held that he was satisfied that the plaintiff made out a good prima facie case for trial and the defendants failed to controvert by any papers in showing that the plaintiffs did not pay more than 300 percent of the principal loan. Upon such view, learned Joint District Judge allowed the application and granted temporary injunction as prayed for. Hence, this appeal. 

 9. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, submitted that learned Joint District Judge failed to notice and decide the moot question as to whether the plaintiffs became defaulters .under the Bank Company Act, 1991 and without deciding such question, he committed serious error in law in granting temporary injunction. 

 10. He submitted that admittedly the plaintiffs were guarantors who undertook to repay the loan including interest as was due against schedule 112 loan accounts by their own decision dated 12-12-93 and they failed to pay Taka 118,46,37,087.31 save paltry amount and defaulted in the payment of the balance in spite of repeated demands, They were therefore, not entitled to any injunction for preventing their names from being published in CIB report. 

 12. Mr Ahsanul Karim, learned Advocate on behalf of the plaintiffs, on the other hand, submitted that as the plaintiffs were mere guarantors and under the Bank Company Act a bank was not entitled and authorised to send the names of such guarantors as defaulters, the learned Joint District Judge correctly granted temporary injunction. 	. 

 13. He submitted that definition of a defaulter as given in the Bank Company Act did not include a guarantor and learned Joint District Judge therefore, committed no error in granting temporary injunction restraining IFIC Bank from sending the names of the plaintiffs as defaulters to the Bangladesh Bank for publication. 

 14. In reply, Mr Mahmudul Islam submitted that the Ain and Bank Company Act are in pari-materia, and the definition of 'loan' as defined in the Ain but not defined by the Bank Company Act included a guarantor as well and, under such definition of 'loan' the plaintiffs were not entitled to prevent their names from being sent to the Bangladesh Bank for publication. 

 16. Whole suit of the plaintiffs is based on the claim that they already paid more than 300 percent of the principal and any claim of the IFIC Bank is now barred under section 47 of the Ain. In support of such claim, the plaintiffs did •not produce any paper or document whatsoever. 

 17. Defendants IFIC Bank, on the other hand, claim that as per decision of the board resolution dated 12-12-93 the plaintiffs undertook to pay Taka 118,46,37,087.31. After payment of some amount out of said sum in different installments, the plaintiffs still owe to pay Taka 135,09,69,535.31 as was due on 31-12-03. 

 18. IFIC Bank also did not produce any paper or document in support of such claims. Who of the plaintiffs or defendants are correct could only be decided at the trial of the suit upon evidence. But the question remains for answer, whether in view of the written objection that the plaintiffs were defaulters on 'the date of suit, were the plaintiffs entitled to temporary injunction as prayed for. 

 19. Without contesting such claim of the IFIC Bank the plaintiffs mainly urged upon the law that guarantors were never included within the definition of defaulters by the Bank Company Act and under section 27(ka)(ka) no bank was therefore, authorised to send the names of guarantors to Bangladesh Bank for publication in the CIB report. 

 22. The question may be seen from another aspect. If the submission of learned Advocate for the plaintiffs that a guarantor would never become a defaulter within the meaning of the Bank Company Act is accepted then the position would be that a guarantor who stood surety and undertook to repay certain bank loan or dues but failed to pay within the time agreed upon, no mechanism or machinery prescribed by such law for recovery of the loan from the borrower would be available to the bank for recovery of the loan from such guarantor. Result being a guarantor would escape his guarantee, which cannot be the intention of the legislature and the security of guarantee loses all, its meaning and purposes. 

 27. In such view of the matter, we are unable to accept the conclusion of the trial Court. The learned Joint District Judge failed to look at the relevant law in deciding the rights of the plaintiffs to temporary injunction. The findings of the trial Court that the plaintiffs' have got a prima facie case and the balance of convenience and inconvenience in their favour are all based upon ignorance of law and cannot be sustained in law. Appeal, accordingly, succeeds.
